subtopic: What drew you to jewellery design
question: What first drew you to jewellery design as a field of study?
lookingFor: A genuine personal moment of discovery tied to hands-on interest, not a vague love of pretty things.

bullets: Name a specific moment or experience that sparked the interest
Show it moved from casual liking to active making or exploring
Connect it to why you want formal training now
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I started making earrings out of beads and wire for my cousin's wedding when I was fourteen, just because we could not afford to buy enough for the whole bridal party. I loved figuring out how to balance the weight so they would not tug at the ear, and that problem solving stuck with me long after the wedding was done. I have been sketching and making small pieces since, but I want proper training in metalwork and stone setting so I can turn what is currently trial and error into real skill.

commonMistakes: Saying 'I have always loved jewellery' with no specific memory
Describing only shopping or collecting jewellery, not making it
Treating the answer as a fashion statement rather than a craft interest
followUps: Do you still have that first piece, and what would you change about it now?

subtopic: Why jewellery design over a related field
question: Why jewellery design specifically, rather than fashion design or fine arts?
lookingFor: Clear articulation of what is unique to jewellery, scale, material, wearability, versus adjacent creative fields.

bullets: Identify what jewellery offers that fashion or fine art does not
Reference the material and technical dimension, not just aesthetics
Show it is a considered choice, not a fallback
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I did think seriously about fashion design because I love garments too, but what pulls me toward jewellery is the scale and the permanence. A piece of jewellery has to work at a few centimetres, every curve and weight distribution matters in a way fabric forgives more easily, and it usually outlives the person who made it. I also like that it sits between craft and engineering, you are literally shaping metal and setting stones, and that hands on precision is what I want to spend years getting good at.

commonMistakes: Giving a vague answer that could apply to any design field
Dismissing the other field instead of explaining the pull toward this one
No mention of material or technical aspects specific to jewellery
followUps: What part of the technical process appeals to you most, metalwork or stone setting?

subtopic: Why this college or program
question: Why do you want to study jewellery design at this institute rather than elsewhere?
lookingFor: Specific, researched reasons tied to the program's studios, faculty, or curriculum, not generic prestige.

bullets: Name a specific studio facility, faculty specialism, or curriculum feature
Connect it to a concrete personal goal or gap in current skill
Show awareness of what makes this program different from alternatives
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I looked at a few programs, but yours is one of the only ones with a dedicated stone setting lab in the first year rather than the third, and setting is exactly the skill I have not been able to teach myself from books. I also read about the collaboration with local goldsmiths for the metalwork module, which matters to me because I want to learn traditional technique before I start relying on CAD. That combination of early hands on training and a link to working craftspeople is what made this my first choice.

commonMistakes: Citing only rankings or reputation
Giving praise so generic it could describe any design school
Confusing this program with a fashion or fine arts program
followUps: What would you want to learn in your first term here?

subtopic: Walking through your portfolio
question: Talk us through one piece in your portfolio, from idea to finished object.
lookingFor: Ability to narrate a design process with real decisions, not just describe the finished look.

bullets: Start from the initial idea or inspiration, not the finished photo
Explain at least one decision or constraint that changed the design along the way
Describe the making process, not only the concept
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The ring I would talk about started from a photo of cracked riverbed clay I took on a school trip, I liked how the irregular lines still felt balanced. My first sketch had the crack pattern running all the way round the band, but when I made a paper mockup it looked too busy on a small ring, so I pulled the pattern back to just the top third. I carved the design in wax, cast it in silver, and then had to file down one edge that came out sharper than I wanted because it was catching on fabric when I wore it.

commonMistakes: Describing only the finished appearance with no process
Claiming everything went perfectly with no adjustments
Being unable to explain a basic technical step involved
followUps: What would you do differently if you made that piece again?

subtopic: A designer or house you admire
question: Is there a jewellery designer or house whose work you particularly admire? What draws you to it?
lookingFor: Informed, specific admiration that shows real engagement with the field, not just a famous name dropped.

bullets: Name a specific designer, house, or body of work
Explain what specifically about their approach or technique appeals to you
Show awareness of their signature style or contribution to the field
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I keep coming back to Suzanne Belperron, mostly because she refused to sign her pieces and said the design itself was the signature, which I find quite bold for someone working in the 1930s and 40s. I love how sculptural her work is, she treated gold almost like clay, letting it fold and swell rather than sitting flat with stones just placed on top. It made me think differently about volume in my own sketches, that jewellery does not have to be flat to read as elegant.

commonMistakes: Naming a brand with no explanation beyond 'I like their style'
Only mentioning price or celebrity association
Picking someone whose actual work they cannot describe
followUps: Can you point to something in your own work influenced by them?

subtopic: Critiquing a piece of jewellery
question: Describe a piece of jewellery you think is badly designed. What would you change?
lookingFor: A constructive critical eye applied to concrete design choices, not just personal taste.

bullets: Pick a real, describable piece rather than a vague category
Identify a specific design or functional flaw, not just 'I don't like it'
Offer a concrete alternative, showing design thinking
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: There was a statement necklace I tried on at a local exhibition that had a beautiful stone cluster, but the clasp sat right at the front of the neck instead of the back, so it dug in whenever you turned your head. The designer had clearly prioritised the visual symmetry of the piece over how it would actually sit on someone. I would have moved the heaviest stones slightly off centre and hidden the clasp at the nape, which would have solved the comfort problem without losing much of the visual impact.

commonMistakes: Giving vague criticism like 'it's just not my taste'
Criticizing something they cannot actually describe in detail
Offering no proposed fix or alternative
followUps: Do you think function should ever be sacrificed for a strong visual statement?

subtopic: Gold purity and the karat system
question: Can you explain what karat means when we talk about gold, and why 24 karat gold is rarely used for everyday jewellery?
lookingFor: Correct basic technical understanding of gold purity and practical reasoning about durability.

bullets: State that karat measures gold purity out of 24 parts
Explain that pure gold is soft, so it is alloyed with other metals for strength
Give an example of a common karat used in jewellery and why
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Karat tells you how much pure gold is in a piece out of 24 parts, so 24 karat is pure gold and 18 karat is 18 parts gold to 6 parts other metals. Pure gold is actually quite soft and bends or scratches easily, which is fine for a coin you keep in a drawer but not for a ring you wear every day. That is why most fine jewellery is 18 karat or lower, the added metals like copper or silver make it hard enough to hold its shape and take daily wear.

commonMistakes: Confusing karat with carat, the gemstone weight unit
Thinking higher karat always means better jewellery
Giving no explanation of why alloying is necessary
followUps: What might 22 karat gold be used for instead of 18?

subtopic: Precious versus semi-precious stones
question: What is the difference between a precious stone and a semi-precious stone?
lookingFor: Correct basic classification with awareness that the distinction is more historical than scientific.

bullets: Name the traditional four precious stones
Note that everything else is generally called semi-precious
Show awareness that the line is more about tradition and value than actual rarity or hardness
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Traditionally there are four precious stones, diamond, ruby, sapphire and emerald, and pretty much every other gemstone like amethyst, garnet or topaz gets called semi-precious. But that split is really historical rather than scientific, some semi-precious stones like fine tanzanite or spinel are rarer and more expensive than a low quality ruby. I try not to lean too hard on the label when I am designing, I think about hardness, colour and cost instead, because those actually affect how I would set and use a stone.

commonMistakes: Listing the four precious stones incorrectly
Treating 'semi-precious' as meaning cheap or low quality
Not knowing the distinction exists at all
followUps: Can you name a semi-precious stone you would like to design around?

subtopic: The 4 Cs of diamond quality
question: What are the 4 Cs used to grade a diamond?
lookingFor: Accurate recall of the four grading criteria with a basic sense of how each affects appearance or value.

bullets: Name all four Cs correctly: carat, cut, colour, clarity
Briefly explain what at least two of them affect
Show understanding that cut affects sparkle more than size does
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The 4 Cs are carat, cut, colour and clarity. Carat is just the weight, colour ranges from colourless to noticeably yellow, and clarity is about internal inclusions you can sometimes see under magnification. I find cut the most interesting of the four because it is the one entirely controlled by human skill rather than nature, and a well cut smaller diamond can actually look more brilliant than a poorly cut larger one because the angles are what bounce the light back to your eye.

commonMistakes: Mixing up 'carat' and 'karat'
Forgetting one of the four Cs
Assuming size alone determines a diamond's value
followUps: Which of the 4 Cs would you prioritise if you were designing on a budget?

subtopic: Traditional jewellery-making techniques
question: Are you familiar with any traditional metalworking techniques like filigree or granulation? Tell us what you know.
lookingFor: Real, if basic, technical familiarity that shows the applicant has looked past design into how jewellery is actually made.

bullets: Correctly describe at least one named technique
Distinguish it from a related technique to show real understanding, not memorised terms
Mention where or how they encountered it, ideally through hands on exposure
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I have read about and tried a basic version of filigree, where you twist fine wires of gold or silver into delicate curling patterns and solder them into an openwork design, it is common in a lot of traditional Cuttack silver work. Granulation is different, that is when tiny beads of metal are fused onto a surface to create texture, like on some ancient Etruscan pieces I saw pictures of. I have only attempted filigree with a local craftsman during a workshop, my wire control is still rough, but I understood immediately why it takes years to get the tension even.

commonMistakes: Confusing filigree and granulation with each other
Naming techniques with no ability to describe what they involve
Claiming expert skill with no actual hands on exposure
followUps: What tools would you need to attempt filigree yourself?

subtopic: Regional or traditional Indian jewellery craft
question: Can you talk about a traditional Indian jewellery craft, like Kundan or Meenakari, that interests you?
lookingFor: Genuine cultural and technical knowledge of a specific craft tradition, not a surface level mention.

bullets: Name a specific craft tradition and roughly where it comes from
Describe what makes the technique distinctive
Explain what personally draws them to it
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Meenakari is the one I keep returning to, it is the enamelling technique associated with Jaipur where coloured glass paste is fused onto gold or silver in fine compartments, often on the reverse of Kundan set pieces so even the hidden side is beautiful. What draws me to it is that idea of hidden craftsmanship, the wearer might never turn the piece over, but the maker still puts in the same care. I would love to eventually combine that philosophy with more contemporary silhouettes, so the detail is not lost even in a simpler design.

commonMistakes: Naming a craft with no idea what it actually involves
Confusing Kundan setting with Meenakari enamelling
Treating Indian craft only as decoration with no context of origin
followUps: How would you adapt that craft for a more minimal, modern piece?

subtopic: CAD and digital tools in modern jewellery design
question: How do you see CAD software fitting into the jewellery design process, alongside traditional hand skills?
lookingFor: Balanced understanding of digital tools as complementary to, not a replacement for, hand craft skill.

bullets: Show awareness of what CAD is actually used for in jewellery, precision modelling and 3D printing masters
Avoid treating CAD as either irrelevant or a full substitute for hand skill
Give a view on when each approach is more useful
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think CAD is brilliant for precision work, resizing a ring accurately or repeating a pattern symmetrically is much faster and more exact on screen than by hand. But I do not think it replaces hand skill, sketching lets me think loosely and make happy accidents that a parametric model does not really allow for, and setting a stone or judging how a curve catches light is still something I want to learn with my hands first. My ideal process would probably be sketch and prototype by hand early on, then use CAD once I know the form I actually want to refine and produce.

commonMistakes: Dismissing CAD entirely as 'not real craft'
Treating CAD as the only serious modern approach and hand skill as outdated
Giving a vague answer with no specific use case for either
followUps: Have you used any CAD software yourself, even briefly?

subtopic: Ethical sourcing and sustainability in jewellery
question: Jewellery design often involves gold mining and gemstone sourcing that can have serious environmental and ethical costs. How would you think about that as a designer?
lookingFor: Genuine awareness of the issue with a considered, non-performative position on the designer's responsibility.

bullets: Show real awareness of specific issues, such as conflict diamonds, mercury use in small scale gold mining, or exploitative labour
Avoid a purely idealistic answer with no acknowledgment of cost or access trade offs
Offer at least one concrete practice a designer could adopt, like recycled metal or traceable sourcing
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I read about the Kimberley Process for diamonds a while ago and then realised it does not actually cover a lot of the harm, like labour conditions or mercury pollution from small scale gold mining, so I try not to treat certification alone as a full answer. As a student designer I know I cannot single handedly fix a global supply chain, but I can make choices like specifying recycled gold where possible and asking suppliers direct questions about sourcing rather than assuming it is fine. I think the honest position is that this is an ongoing responsibility, not a box you tick once.

commonMistakes: Giving a vague statement that sustainability 'matters to me' with no specifics
Claiming certification alone solves the problem
Dismissing the issue as something only large companies need to worry about
followUps: Would you be willing to design with a more limited material palette to keep sourcing traceable?

subtopic: Personal design process from concept to prototype
question: Walk us through how you typically move from an initial idea to a wearable prototype.
lookingFor: A real, ordered process that shows iteration, not a single leap from sketch to finished piece.

bullets: Describe an actual sequence of stages, not just 'I sketch and then I make it'
Mention at least one intermediate step like a mockup, scale test, or material trial
Show willingness to revise based on what the mockup reveals
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I usually start with quick thumbnail sketches, a whole page of small versions rather than one perfect drawing, because the fifth or sixth idea is often better than the first. Once something feels promising I make a paper or card mockup at actual size and try wearing it, which tells me things a flat sketch never can, like whether a pendant will sit flat or twist around. Only after that do I move to metal, usually starting in a cheaper material like copper or brass before committing to silver or gold, because I would rather waste an inexpensive metal on a mistake than a precious one.

commonMistakes: Skipping straight from idea to final material with no testing stage
Giving a vague description with no concrete steps
Not acknowledging that the process involves revision
followUps: What do you do when the prototype does not match your sketch?

subtopic: Balancing aesthetics with wearability and comfort
question: How do you balance a striking visual design with the practical need for a piece to actually be comfortable and durable to wear?
lookingFor: Understanding that jewellery is a functional wearable object, with real consideration of weight, edges, and daily use.

bullets: Acknowledge specific practical factors, weight distribution, sharp edges, clasp placement, prong security
Show that this is a real design constraint, not an afterthought
Give a concrete example of a trade off they navigated
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I designed a cuff with an angular geometric edge that looked great in my sketch, but when I made a card mockup it caught on sleeves every time I moved my arm. I did not want to lose the angularity entirely because that was the whole character of the piece, so I softened just the two edges that made contact with clothing and kept the rest sharp. I think good jewellery design is really about deciding which parts of a strong idea are non negotiable and which parts need to bend for comfort, rather than assuming you have to pick one or the other.

commonMistakes: Treating comfort and durability as unimportant compared to visual impact
Giving no concrete example of an actual trade off
Overcorrecting into a purely safe, boring design with no visual ambition
followUps: Have you ever made something that turned out to be uncomfortable to wear? What did you learn?

subtopic: Costume jewellery versus fine jewellery
question: What is the difference between costume jewellery and fine jewellery?
lookingFor: Correct basic understanding of material and market distinctions between the two categories.

bullets: Correctly identify that fine jewellery uses precious metals and genuine gemstones
Note that costume jewellery uses base metals and imitation materials, often for fashion rather than investment value
Show awareness that both require genuine design skill, one is not simply lesser
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Fine jewellery is made with precious metals like gold, silver or platinum and genuine gemstones, so it holds real material value and is usually meant to last generations. Costume jewellery uses base metals, plating and often glass or synthetic stones, so it is much more affordable and tends to follow fast fashion trends more closely. I do not think that makes costume jewellery a lesser design challenge though, if anything working within cheaper materials forces you to be more inventive with form and finish since you cannot rely on the material's own value to carry the piece.

commonMistakes: Assuming costume jewellery requires no real design skill
Confusing plated metal with solid precious metal
Giving no mention of the underlying material difference
followUps: Which would you rather design for as a student, and why?

subtopic: Colour theory and pairing stones with metal
question: How would you think about pairing a gemstone's colour with a particular metal in a design?
lookingFor: Applied colour theory reasoning specific to jewellery, not just generic art class colour wheel recitation.

bullets: Reference basic colour theory concepts like warm and cool tones or complementary colours
Apply it specifically to metal and stone combinations, not just abstract colour
Show awareness that skin tone or occasion can also affect the choice
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think about warm and cool tones first, yellow gold tends to sit better with warmer stones like citrine or a warm toned ruby, while white gold or platinum can make a cool blue sapphire or an icy diamond feel crisper. But I also think about contrast, a deep emerald against yellow gold can look richer than against white metal because the warm tone intensifies the green rather than competing with it. I would want to see the actual stone and metal together though, photographs never quite capture how they read against each other in real light.

commonMistakes: Reciting the colour wheel with no application to actual jewellery materials
Ignoring how metal tone interacts with stone colour
Treating the choice as purely personal taste with no reasoning
followUps: Would your answer change if you were designing for someone with a cooler skin undertone?

subtopic: Basic jewellery-making tools
question: Can you name a few basic hand tools used in jewellery making and what they are for?
lookingFor: Real familiarity with hands on craft, not purely theoretical design interest.

bullets: Name at least two or three actual tools correctly
Briefly explain what each is used for
Show this comes from some direct exposure, not just reading
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A jeweller's saw is what you use to cut shapes out of sheet metal, it has a very fine blade so you can follow tight curves. A mandrel is the tapered metal rod you use to shape and size rings, you hammer the metal round it to get an even circle. I have also used flat and round nose pliers for bending wire, the round nose ones are what let you make an even loop rather than a kinked angle. I picked most of this up during a short workshop, my saw control especially still needs a lot of practice.

commonMistakes: Naming tools with no idea what they are actually for
Confusing basic tools, like a mandrel and a burnisher
Claiming fluency with no real hands on exposure at all
followUps: Which of those tools have you actually had the chance to use yourself?

subtopic: Building inspiration or a mood board
question: Where do you usually find inspiration for a new design, and how do you turn that into something concrete?
lookingFor: A genuine, specific source of inspiration paired with a real method for translating it into design, not just 'everywhere'.

bullets: Name a specific, personal source of inspiration rather than a vague generality
Describe an actual method for capturing or developing it, like a mood board or sketch series
Show the link between the inspiration and an actual design outcome
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I keep a small notebook I carry around and sketch or note down things that catch my eye, it is often quite ordinary, the way light comes through a fan blade or the pattern on a leaf that has started to curl and dry. When something keeps coming back to mind after a few days, I know it is worth developing, so I will pull together a few photos and sketches into a mood board and start looking for the actual repeatable shape or line in it. My leaf design series for my portfolio came directly from a dried banyan leaf I picked up on a walk and kept on my desk for weeks.

commonMistakes: Saying inspiration comes from 'everything' with no specific example
Describing no method for turning inspiration into an actual design
Naming a source with no connection to any real piece they made
followUps: Do you keep a sketchbook or visual journal regularly?

subtopic: Designing for a specific client or occasion
question: Imagine a client asks you to design an engagement ring for someone who is very active and works with their hands often. How would you approach that brief?
lookingFor: Practical design thinking that adapts aesthetic choices to a real functional constraint.

bullets: Identify the core practical constraint, durability and low snag risk
Suggest concrete design choices, like a lower profile setting or a harder stone
Show they would still want to understand the client's taste, not just solve for function alone
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The first thing I would want to know is more about her taste, but functionally I would steer away from tall prong settings that catch on gloves or fabric, and probably suggest a bezel or low set style that protects the stone's edges. I would also think about the stone itself, a softer gem like an opal would scratch easily with daily hand use, so I might suggest sapphire or a well cut diamond instead if she wants something that can genuinely take a beating. I would want to show her a couple of options rather than assume, because plenty of people with active hands still want a dramatic silhouette and are willing to take the ring off for certain tasks.

commonMistakes: Ignoring the practical constraint entirely and designing purely for looks
Overcorrecting into an overly plain design with no attempt at personality
Not asking about the client's own preferences at all
followUps: What would you do if the client insisted on a tall setting anyway?

subtopic: A historical jewellery period or style
question: Can you tell us about a historical period of jewellery design that you find interesting, like Art Deco or Mughal jewellery?
lookingFor: Genuine, specific historical knowledge connected to visual characteristics, not just naming a period.

bullets: Name a specific period or tradition and roughly when or where it flourished
Describe at least one visual or technical characteristic that defines it
Explain what personally draws them to it
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I am quite drawn to Art Deco jewellery from the 1920s and 30s, the geometric symmetry and the way it combined materials like onyx and platinum with diamonds to get such sharp contrast. It came out of a period fascinated with speed and machinery, and you can really see that in the clean angular lines, it is such a departure from the flowing organic curves of Art Nouveau just before it. I like it because it feels disciplined, every line seems intentional, and I think that restraint is something I want to bring into my own more maximalist tendencies.

commonMistakes: Naming a period with no actual visual characteristics described
Getting basic chronology or geography wrong
Treating it as purely decorative history with no connection to their own interest
followUps: Do you see any of that influence in jewellery being made today?

subtopic: 3D printing and rapid prototyping trade-offs
question: What do you see as the trade-offs between 3D printing a design and handcrafting it traditionally?
lookingFor: Nuanced understanding of both approaches' strengths and limitations, not a one sided verdict.

bullets: Identify at least one genuine advantage of 3D printing, speed, precision, repeatability
Identify at least one genuine advantage of handcraft, texture, imperfection, tactile decision making
Avoid declaring one approach simply superior overall
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: 3D printing is fantastic for precision and speed, if I need to test five variations of a ring's proportions or want a symmetrical repeated pattern, printing a wax or resin master saves an enormous amount of time compared to carving each one by hand. But it can also flatten a design in a way, the surface comes out very uniform, and some of the character that comes from a hand carved wax, the tiny irregularities, gets lost unless you deliberately design them back in. I think the honest answer is that they suit different stages, printing for iteration and precision, handwork for the final character and finish, and a good designer probably uses both depending on the piece.

commonMistakes: Declaring one method categorically better with no nuance
Giving a vague answer with no specific advantage named for either method
Treating 3D printing as something only used for cheap jewellery
followUps: Would you use 3D printing for a one off custom piece, or only for repeated production?

subtopic: Redesigning under a material or budget constraint
question: If you had designed a piece using a particular gemstone, and then found out the client's budget could not stretch to it, how would you handle that?
lookingFor: Pragmatic, creative problem solving under constraint that preserves the design intent rather than treating budget as a dead end.

bullets: Show willingness to revisit the design rather than simply refusing or resenting the constraint
Suggest a concrete alternative, a different stone, smaller size, or altered setting
Demonstrate they would still try to protect what made the original design work
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I would first work out what the stone was actually doing in the design, was it the colour, the size, or the way it caught light, because that tells me what I actually need to preserve. If it was the deep blue of a sapphire that mattered most, I might suggest a lab grown sapphire or a well cut blue topaz instead, which keeps the colour story intact at a fraction of the cost. I would rather have that honest conversation and offer real alternatives than quietly downgrade the whole design and hope the client does not notice the difference.

commonMistakes: Treating the budget constraint as something to simply accept without creative response
Suggesting a substitute with no explanation of what quality it preserves
Assuming the client would rather abandon the design than adapt it
followUps: Would you tell the client outright that the substitute is not the same, or let the finished piece speak for itself?

subtopic: Designing for a target customer or market segment
question: When you design a collection, how much do you think about who would actually wear or buy it?
lookingFor: Awareness that jewellery design sits within a market context, without losing personal design voice entirely.

bullets: Show they consider a real audience, not just designing purely for self expression
Balance that awareness against keeping a personal design voice
Give a concrete example connecting a design decision to an intended wearer
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think about it quite a lot, actually, because a piece nobody would wear is really just sculpture, and I do want people to wear my work. For my last collection I was designing for someone like my older sister, someone in her late twenties who wants something distinctive for work but cannot wear anything too loud in a formal office, so I kept the silhouettes clean but let the texture do the interesting work instead of scale or colour. I do not think that market awareness has to mean losing your own voice, it just means being specific about who you are speaking to instead of designing for an imagined nobody.

commonMistakes: Claiming to design purely for themselves with no thought of a wearer
Treating market awareness as pure commercialism with no design integrity
Giving a vague description of an audience with no specific design decisions tied to it
followUps: Has thinking about a specific wearer ever changed a design you were attached to?

subtopic: Learning from a failed piece or mistake
question: Tell us about a piece that did not turn out the way you planned. What happened, and what did you take from it?
lookingFor: Honest account of a real technical or design failure with genuine reflection and change in approach.

bullets: Describe a specific, real failure, not a disguised success
Explain what actually went wrong, technically or in judgement
Show a concrete change made afterward as a result
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I once tried to solder a delicate filigree pendant and overheated one section, the fine wire just melted and slumped before I noticed, and I had to scrap almost a week of work. It was frustrating, but it taught me that I had been rushing the heat control because I was excited to finish, rather than watching the metal closely enough as it changed colour. Since then I heat test on scrap wire first whenever I am trying a technique I am not fully confident in, and I have not lost a piece to overheating since.

commonMistakes: Describing a 'failure' that is secretly a humble brag
Blaming tools or materials with no personal reflection
Giving no concrete change in practice described afterward
followUps: How do you decide when a piece is worth salvaging versus starting over?
